cards.explanation: The answer is that they have not prevailed against Israel. Israel says, "…but they have not prevailed against me." (Psalm 129:2) Persecuted many a time, and still standing. Notice the "but" in the middle of that verse, friends, because that little word is doing a LOT of heavy lifting.

The answer is False. The psalm says, "The plowmen plowed over my back; they made their furrows long." (Psalm 129:3) Long furrows, not short ones. One little word, friends, and it changes the whole picture.

The answer is True, and listen to how plain it is. "The LORD is righteous…" (Psalm 129:4) After the plowmen and the long furrows, Israel doesn't grumble. Israel says who the LORD is. That's some steady faith right there.

The answer is that the LORD cut Israel from the cords of the wicked. "The LORD is righteous; He has cut me from the cords of the wicked." (Psalm 129:4) Cords are what tie something down, and the psalm says He cut Israel loose from them. The verse names the LORD as the One who did the cutting. I've been tied up in a few tight spots myself, friends, so I know a good snip when I hear one.

The answer is that they be turned back in shame. The psalm says, "May all who hate Zion be turned back in shame." (Psalm 129:5) It's a wish, not a report, friends. Zion is the city of Jerusalem, and the ones who hate it are the ones in the wish.

The answer is withers. "May they be like grass on the rooftops, which withers before it can grow…" (Psalm 129:6) The grass never gets the chance to grow. That's the picture the psalm wishes on those who hate Zion.

The answer is "The blessing of the LORD be on you." The psalm says, "May none who pass by say to them, “The blessing of the LORD be on you; we bless you in the name of the LORD.”" (Psalm 129:8) So the wish is that no one passing by would speak that blessing over them. That's how the song ends, friends.
